title: Implement Selection Sort: find the smallest element, put it first, then find next smallest, put it second, repeat; O(n^2).
keyPoints: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum in the unsorted suffix and swaps it into the next sorted position.
It performs at most n - 1 swaps, the fewest of all simple sorts, minimising write operations.
Time is O(n^2) in all cases because it always scans the full unsorted suffix; there is no early exit.
The basic version is not stable because a long-distance swap can jump equal elements past each other.
Space is O(1) since it sorts entirely in place with only a temporary variable.
Its niche is when writes are expensive (flash memory, large records) because it minimises swaps.
For production use, Java's library sorts are always preferred over hand-written selection sort.

s1_definition.oneliner: Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next sorted position.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Selection sort** – divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix, growing the prefix one element at a time.
- **Find minimum** – each pass scans the unsorted suffix to find the index of the minimum element.
- **Single swap** – one swap per pass places the minimum at the front of the unsorted region.
- **Minimal writes** – at most n - 1 swaps total, the fewest of all simple sorts.
- **Not stable** – the basic version is unstable because long-distance swaps can reorder equal elements.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India lining up account balances from smallest to largest. The clerk scans the entire pile to find the single smallest balance and places it firmly at the front. Then she scans the remaining pile to find the next smallest and places it second. She repeats, each time selecting the minimum of what is left and locking it into the next position.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Selection Sort Pass-by-Pass:

  [75000, 25000, 50000, 10000]
   ^sorted|----unsorted------^

  Pass 1: scan unsorted, find min = 10000 at index 3
    swap arr[0] <-> arr[3]
  [10000, 25000, 50000, 75000]
   ^--sorted--|---unsorted---^

  Pass 2: scan unsorted, find min = 25000 at index 1
    already in place, no swap
  [10000, 25000, 50000, 75000]
   ^----sorted----|--unsorted^

  Pass 3: scan unsorted, find min = 50000 at index 2
    already in place
  [10000, 25000, 50000, 75000]
   ^------sorted------|------^

  Done! Sorted prefix covers entire array.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Selection sort divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix. On each pass it scans the unsorted suffix to find the minimum element and swaps it into the first unsorted position, growing the sorted prefix by one. It has O(n^2) time in every case, uses O(1) extra memory, and the basic version is not stable.

Its distinguishing feature is the swap count. Selection sort performs exactly one swap per pass, at most n - 1 swaps total, which is the fewest of all simple sorts. When writes are expensive, such as on flash memory or with large objects costly to copy, selection sort minimises the number of moves.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, selection sort is useful only conceptually for ordering a small set of flagged accounts from smallest to largest balance. In any production system, the library sort is always the right choice.

The honest senior-level assessment is that selection sort's quadratic comparisons make it unsuitable for large data, and its instability is a limitation. Its genuine niches are tiny arrays and write-minimising scenarios.

Remember one sentence: selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted remainder and places it next, performing the fewest swaps of any simple sort but always doing quadratic comparisons.
